chapter_theme: Verses 41 to 60 count, three at a time, what heads instruction, what makes a family fair or brings it down, what leads to hell or stops the rain, what the wise avoid and what is wasted, and close on the sorrow proper to every kind of birth; household, royal and inward conduct are judged on one scale.

41.reading: Renown from giving something to those in distress, the worth that keeps one's family standing from sinking even when shaken, and adding to one's friends day by day with affection are named the three chief of all that is heard.
41.nuance: The predicate கேள்வியுள் எல்லாந் தலை ranks three practices above everything learnt by hearing, so the verse measures instruction by what it should make a person do; the second item concedes that the family may be shaken (துளங்கினும்) and asks only that its worth not fall.

items.claim: renown won by giving to the distressed is chief among things heard
the worth that keeps one's family standing from declining, even in upheaval, is chief among things heard
increasing one's friends day after day, with affection, is chief among things heard

42.reading: Not coveting wealth that comes from the gaming hall, behaving toward brahmins as toward fire even when familiar with them, and living with a love of farming are said to be the beauty of the vellala family.
42.nuance: பார்ப்பார் is a birth-group term and the rule ranks it: the cultivating family is to keep the distance and caution one keeps with fire however close the acquaintance. The verse defines a family's beauty by occupation and by its bearing toward another birth-group, beside a refusal of gambling gain.

items.claim: not desiring wealth won at the gaming hall is the vellala family's beauty
treating brahmins with the caution due to fire, even when familiar, is reported as the vellala family's beauty
living with a love of farming is the vellala family's beauty

norm.note: a birth-rank rule of the period: the conduct a cultivating family is to keep toward brahmins

43.reading: Restraint of the mouth is purity, restraint of deed without stain is the divine state, and restraint of the heart without falsehood is release; these three are things free of deceit.
43.nuance: The three restraints rise in order, mouth, deed, heart, and their fruits rise with them, from purity to the heavenly (திப்பியம்) to release (வீடு), so the verse is a ladder rather than a list of equals. மாசற்ற may also be read with துப்புரவாம் (stainless purity) rather than with செய்கை.

items.claim: restraint of the mouth is purity
restraint of action, without stain, is the divine state
restraint of the heart, without falsehood, is release

44.reading: A day on which one ate without a guest, a night on which one did not turn to embrace one's well-adorned wife, and a morning on which one went off without giving to the needy are a sickness to the strong-minded.
44.nuance: The three items run through the whole day, day, night and morning (பகல், கங்குல், காலை), so the householder's day is judged complete only when guest, wife and the poor have each had their share; the sickness falls on உரனுடையார், the strong, as if neglect were felt only by those fit to do these duties.

items.claim: a day on which one ate with no guest is a sickness to the strong
a night on which one did not turn to embrace one's well-adorned wife is a sickness to the strong
a morning on which one left without giving something to those who have nothing is a sickness to the strong

45.reading: The one who torments a man who cannot do a thing by telling him to do it, the one who without love hides from those who ask what he could give, and the one who does not think on the certainty of Death's coming are three who fall into hell.
45.nuance: The third man has done nothing to anyone: forgetting death is set beside cruelty and concealment as an offence of equal weight, so heedlessness itself earns hell.

items.claim: one who harasses a person unable to act by ordering him to act falls into hell
one who, without love, hides from askers what he could give falls into hell
one who does not reflect that Death's coming is certain falls into hell

46.reading: A spirited horse whose feet are not sound, a fierce elephant with no clean seat above, and the place of one who snarls, nurses rancour and speaks in rage are three things the wise do not go near.
46.nuance: கால்தூய்மை and மேல்தூய்மை are obscure: they may mean a horse not sure of foot and an elephant with no trained rider on its back, or untamed beasts generally. பள்ளி may be the angry man's dwelling or his company. The verse sets an angry man among dangerous animals.

items.claim: a spirited horse without soundness of foot is not approached by the wise
a fierce elephant without cleanness above is not approached by the wise
the place of one who rages and speaks in anger is not approached by the wise

47.reading: Women of few words and broad shoulders, the choice wealth one has brought in by many kinds of effort, and food prepared so that it makes the tongue flourish are three things whose guarding must not be slighted.
47.nuance: Women are counted among the goods of the house with earned treasure and good food, all three needing watch; the verse reports the custodial view of women of its period. காப்பிகழ் ஆகா may also be read as 'not to be scorned', which would make the line a praise of the three rather than a rule of keeping them.

items.claim: women of few words and broad shoulders are, the verse says, not to be left unguarded
choice wealth earned by one's own effort is not to be left unguarded
food prepared to delight the tongue is not to be left unguarded

norm.note: a household norm of the period that counts women among the goods a man must guard

48.reading: The one who takes abuse as sweet speech, the one who values gruel as rice poured with ghee, and the one who eats seeping bitterness accepting it as sugar are three who live having seen the true thing.
48.nuance: Each item takes a bad thing as its opposite, in speech, in food and in taste, and the verse calls this not endurance but sight of the true (மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டு): the bitter is not borne as bitter, it is no longer judged so.

items.claim: one who takes abuse as sweet words lives having seen the truth
one who esteems gruel as ghee-rice lives having seen the truth
one who eats bitterness accepting it as sugar lives having seen the truth

49.reading: Young kin who set aside what they are bidden, a head of the house who keeps no guard and speaks in abuse and scorn, and a wife who wears that house down through falsehood are three who are no security for this life.
49.nuance: ஏவாது மாற்றும் may mean 'refuses without being asked' or 'sets aside the bidding'; பொய்தெள்ளி ('sifting falsehood') is unclear. The verse spreads the failure of a house over its junior, its head and its wife, each by a fault of speech or obedience.

items.claim: young kin who set aside what they are bidden are no security for this life
a head of house who, unguarding, speaks in abuse and contempt is no security for this life
a wife who wears down that house through falsehood is, the verse says, no security for this life

norm.note: a judgment of the period on a wife's conduct in the house, set beside those on kin and husband

50.reading: A king who covets goods to seize and harasses his people, men of deceitful speech who do not say what is within, and a woman who, living in the house, crosses its bounds are three ill planets that swiftly cut off the rain.
50.nuance: கோள் is a malign planet: the verse gives three human faults the astrological power to stop rain, ranging from the throne through common men to a wife, so the cosmic sanction the Kural gives to the king is spread over the whole society.

items.claim: a king who covets plunder and harasses his subjects swiftly cuts off the rain
men of deceitful speech who hide the truth swiftly cut off the rain
a woman who, being of the house, crosses its bounds is said to cut off the rain

norm.note: a rule of the period binding a wife's conduct to the household's bounds, and her transgression to drought

51.reading: Allies remain allies even when they keep their distance, deceivers remain deceivers even when they keep close, and the base are hurtful like a split stone; these three, when examined, show what they are.
51.nuance: தூர்ந்துஒழுகி is obscure: read with தூரா in verse 56 it means 'when the way is closed', so the ally stays an ally even when estranged. ஈர்ந்தகல் may be a sawn stone that cannot rejoin, an image for the base. The point is constancy of nature under changed conduct.

items.claim: true allies remain allies even when estranged
deceivers remain deceivers even when they keep close
the base are hurtful, like a split stone

52.reading: Kindly regard is the ornament of the eye, modesty the ornament of a woman in love, and learning the ornament for the life to come; these three are found only in those who bear the mark of worth.
52.nuance: Each item has its own wearer (the eye, a woman, the next life), and the closing line gathers them: the three are not acquired apart but are found together in the குறியுடையார். The modesty item assigns naanam to women specifically.

items.claim: kindly regard is the ornament of the eye
modesty is, the verse says, the ornament of a woman in love
learning is the ornament for the next world

norm.note: a gender norm of the period: modesty assigned as the woman's ornament

53.reading: The beauty of a blind man's wife, the eager talk of a man without learning that clears darkness, and listening to the lute by one who cannot tell its modes are three things that come to nothing when weighed.
53.nuance: Two items are waste on the receiver's side (beauty unseen, music unheard), and the middle one, the unlearned man's eager speech, is put among them: his talk is like a gift with no one able to take it, or a skill with nothing behind it.

items.claim: the beauty of a blind man's wife comes to nothing
the hasty speech of a man without learned understanding comes to nothing
lute-listening by one who cannot tell the modes comes to nothing

54.reading: Attaching oneself to those who do not weigh one's good, speaking of benefits one will not yield oneself in a moment of anger, and charging others with faults when the charge bears no later fruit are the doings of those without clear sense.
54.nuance: The lines are compressed and each item admits more than one parse (தன்பயம் may be one's own good or the other's; காய்வின்கண் may be 'in anger' or 'toward the angry'). The common thread is action without regard to its result, which the closing word தெற்றெனவு (clarity) names.

items.claim: attaching oneself to those who do not weigh one's good is the work of the unclear
speaking of good benefits in anger is the work of the unclear
charging others with faults that bring no later good is the work of the unclear

55.reading: A friendship that does not keep a weighty secret, a woman who has abandoned the wish for honour, and a petty servant who nurses rancour wherever he is are three who are called spies.
55.nuance: ஒற்றாள் here is not the king's agent but the leak inside one's own circle: friend, woman and servant become informers against the one they are close to. The woman item reports a judgment of the period on women's honour.

items.claim: a friendship that does not keep a deep secret is a spy
a woman who has given up the wish for honour is, the verse says, a spy
a petty servant who acts out of rancour is a spy

norm.note: a judgment of the period that counts a woman without regard for honour among informers

56.reading: First learning the letters as they come, then serving father and mother, and joining the great road of conduct handed down are the three ways by which the path of excellence is not blocked.
56.nuance: முந்தை and பிற்பாடு make this a sequence of life, not a list: letters first, then the parents, then inherited conduct; and the predicate is negative, these keep the road of விழுப்பம் from being choked (தூரா).

items.claim: learning the letters first keeps the path of excellence open
serving father and mother afterward keeps the path of excellence open
joining the great road of inherited conduct keeps the path of excellence open

57.reading: Song not measured to the beat, the clamour of one who enters to beg and eat, and a lodger's craving for the vessels his host uses are three things painful to hear.
57.nuance: தட்டித்து and துச்சிருந்தான் ஆளும் கலம் are hard: the second item may be a beggar knocking and shouting, the third a guest in borrowed quarters who covets the master's vessels. The frame கேள்வியுள் echoes verse 41, which names what is best to hear.

items.claim: song not measured to the beat is painful to hear
the shouting of one who enters to beg his food is painful to hear
a lodger's coveting the vessels his host uses is painful to hear

58.reading: Giving with regard to old ties, embracing kin by right so that they rejoice, and gathering one's people with close words are the work of the king's younger.
58.domain_note: the king's younger brother or junior prince
58.nuance: The kin-work is assigned not to the king but to the one younger than him: holding the royal kin together is a delegated office. இளையான் may be the younger brother or any junior in the royal line.

items.claim: giving with regard to long acquaintance is the king's younger's work
embracing kin by right so that they rejoice is the king's younger's work
gathering his people with close, kinly words is the king's younger's work

59.reading: The wealth of one who does not help his kin, the farming of one who does not tend the green crop at ripening, and the family standing of one who lives drinking toddy while young perish while seeming to exist.
59.nuance: உள்ளன போலக் கெடும் says the ruin is hidden: each thing still appears to be there while it is already lost, so the verse warns against judging by possession.

items.claim: the wealth of one who does not help his kin perishes while seeming to exist
the farming of one who does not guard the crop at ripening perishes while seeming to exist
the family standing of one who drinks toddy from youth perishes while seeming to exist

60.reading: Great hunger in the birth of a ghost, fear in the birth of a beast, and the misery of want in the birth of humans who cannot discern are three that make birth a birth of sorrow.
60.nuance: Each kind of birth is given its own sorrow, so no birth escapes: the human's is not hunger or fear but want (நிரப்பிடும்பை), and புலம்தெரியா makes it the lot of humans who cannot see clearly.

items.claim: great hunger in a ghost's birth makes birth sorrow
fear in an animal's birth makes birth sorrow
the misery of want in human birth makes birth sorrow

links.note: Kural 955 says an old family does not part from its nature even when its means of giving shrink; Thirikadugam makes the worth that keeps family standing from falling, even when shaken, one of three things chief among all that is heard.
links.teaches: The couplet observes that old families hold firm; the verse turns that observation into a thing to be taught and ranked first, so constancy of lineage becomes the content of instruction, not only its result.
links.list_adds: It ranks family constancy with renown from giving to the distressed and with daily widening of friendship, so lineage is made one of three practices that head all teaching.

links.note: Kural 691 tells those who serve kings to be like men warming at a fire, neither near nor far; Thirikadugam tells the vellala family to behave toward brahmins as toward fire even when familiar.
links.teaches: The ethics group uses one fire image for two powers: the Kural for the king, the Thirikadugam for the brahmin, so the cultivator's caution toward a birth-group is modelled on the courtier's caution toward the throne.
links.list_adds: It sets the fire-caution among a farming family's marks of beauty, between refusing gambling wealth and loving the plough, so a rule of birth-rank becomes part of a household's grace.

links.note: Kural 1033 says only those who live by ploughing truly live; Thirikadugam makes love of farming the beauty of one family, the vellala.
links.teaches: The couplet gives ploughing to anyone who will live independently; the verse ties its honour to one birth-group, so the same praise of farming reads in one book as a way of life open to all and in the other as a family's mark.
links.list_adds: It joins love of farming to two other rules for the same family, so the plough becomes one of three marks of a caste-occupation rather than a universal claim.

links.note: Verse 12 defines the vellalan as one who does not eat while a guest waits; verse 42 names three other marks of the vellala family's beauty.
links.teaches: Read together, the book defines the vellala by four conducts, hospitality, refusing gambling gain, caution toward brahmins and love of the plough, so the title is built from conduct and occupation together.

links.note: Kural 127 says guard the tongue whatever else goes unguarded; Thirikadugam makes restraint of the mouth only the first of three restraints, yielding purity, below restraint of deed and of heart.
links.teaches: The Kural puts the tongue first as the one thing to guard; the verse ranks it lowest of three, so what the Kural sets as the minimum the verse treats as the first rung toward release.
links.list_adds: It turns restraint into an ascending ladder, mouth, deed, heart, with a rising fruit at each rung, a ranking the couplet does not make.

links.note: Kural 121 says restraint leads among the immortals; Thirikadugam gives the heavenly state only to restraint of deed and reserves release for restraint of heart.
links.teaches: The couplet's single reward of restraint, a place among the gods, becomes in the verse the middle of three rewards, so heaven is placed below release.
links.list_adds: It splits the Kural's one restraint into three with three fruits, purity, the divine state and release, ranking them.

links.note: Kural 82 says eating alone while a guest waits outside is not to be wished even if the food is ambrosia; Thirikadugam calls a day on which one ate without a guest a sickness to the strong.
links.teaches: The couplet rejects the guestless meal before eating; the verse counts its cost afterwards as an illness, so the same refusal is given both a motive and a symptom.
links.list_adds: It sets the guestless day beside the unembraced night and the morning without giving, so hospitality becomes one of three duties that together fill the householder's whole day.

links.note: Verse 12 says the vellalan does not eat while a guest waits; verse 44 says a day eaten without a guest is a sickness.
links.teaches: The book treats the guestless meal twice, once as a loss of the title vellalan and once as a sickness of the strong, so the same fault is a loss of rank and of health.

links.note: Kural 1067 begs beggars not to beg of those who conceal; Thirikadugam sends the one who without love hides from askers what he could give into hell.
links.teaches: The couplet speaks to the beggar and protects him from the concealer; the verse speaks of the concealer and names his punishment, so the two together cover both sides of the refused request.
links.list_adds: It sets concealment from askers between tormenting the unable and forgetting death, so withholding is ranked with cruelty and heedlessness as a road to hell.

links.note: Naladiyar 20 urges keeping Death's stealth in mind and taking provisions in time; Thirikadugam names not reflecting on Death's certain coming as one of three things that lead to hell.
links.teaches: The quatrain makes remembering death prudent; the verse makes forgetting it a sin with a penalty, so heedlessness is turned from folly into guilt.
links.list_adds: It places forgetting death beside two acts against others, so an inward lapse is judged on the same scale as cruelty and concealment.

links.note: Verse 14 names youth, folly and meanness as three the wise do not approach; verse 46, with the same closing line, names an unsound horse, a fierce elephant and the place of an angry man.
links.teaches: Read together, the book's 'the wise do not go near' covers both inner dispositions and outer dangers, and the angry man of verse 46 stands at the join, a human fault treated like a dangerous beast.

links.note: Kural 57 says the guarding of women by confinement achieves nothing and their own steadfastness is the best guard; Thirikadugam counts women among three things whose guarding must not be slighted. The tension holds on reading காப்பு in 47 as the householder's watch over women.
links.teaches: The two books disagree on who keeps a woman's virtue: the Kural moves the guard inside her and calls custody useless, the Thirikadugam keeps it with the man as with his wealth and food.
links.list_adds: It ranks women with earned treasure and good food as goods to be watched, which is the custodial view the couplet sets aside.

links.note: Kural 159 says those who bear the harsh words of transgressors are as pure as renouncers; Thirikadugam says the one who takes abuse as sweet speech lives having seen the true thing.
links.teaches: The couplet praises bearing abuse as endurance; the verse goes further and has abuse heard as sweetness, so the pair shows two grades, enduring the bitter and no longer tasting it as bitter.
links.list_adds: It sets taking abuse as sweet beside taking gruel as ghee-rice and bitterness as sugar, so patience in speech becomes one case of a general reversal of taste.

links.note: Kural 1065 says even thin gruel is sweetest when earned by one's own effort; Thirikadugam says the one who values gruel as ghee-rice has seen the truth.
links.teaches: The Kural makes gruel sweet because it is one's own; the verse makes it sweet because the seer no longer ranks foods, so one ground is self-respect and the other indifference.
links.list_adds: It puts the gruel among three reversals of speech and taste, so its sweetness comes from a way of seeing, not from how it was earned.

links.note: Kural 52 says if the wife lacks household excellence the life is nothing whatever else it has; Thirikadugam names a wife who wears the house down by falsehood as one of three who are no security for this life.
links.teaches: The couplet lays the failure of the household on the wife alone; the verse sets beside her the disobedient junior and the abusive head, so the pair shows the house can be ruined from three places.
links.list_adds: It distributes the household's ruin across junior kin, the head and the wife, rather than resting it on the wife as the couplet does.

links.note: Kural 559 says the sky withholds rain when the king bends justice; Thirikadugam names the plundering king as one of three malign planets that stop the rain.
links.teaches: The couplet ties rain to the king alone; the verse adds deceitful men and a transgressing wife, so the power to cause drought, a royal burden in the Kural, is spread over common people and the household.
links.list_adds: It sets the king beside commoners and a wife as equal causes of drought, widening the couplet's royal sanction to the whole society.

links.note: Kural 55 says the wife who worships her husband makes it rain at her word; Thirikadugam says the wife who crosses the bounds of the house cuts the rain off.
links.teaches: Together the two books give the period's belief in both directions, a chaste wife commands rain and a transgressing one stops it, so the wife's conduct is treated as a lever on the weather.
links.list_adds: It sets the wife's transgression beside the king's plunder and men's deceit, so her fault is ranked with misrule as a cause of drought.

links.note: Kural 822 says the friendship of those who seem kin but are not shifts like a changing mind; Thirikadugam says deceivers stay deceivers even when they keep close.
links.teaches: The couplet stresses that false friendship changes; the verse that the false friend's nature does not, so the pair separates the shifting surface of conduct from the fixed nature beneath it.
links.list_adds: It sets the deceiver against the true ally who stays an ally even when estranged, so the list gives a test of constancy in both directions.

links.note: Kural 575 says kindly regard is the ornament of the eye and without it the eye is a sore; Thirikadugam opens with the same ornament and says it is found only with modesty and learning in those of worth.
links.teaches: The couplet judges the eye by kindly regard; the verse says that regard is not found alone but in the same people as modesty and learning, so it becomes a sign of a whole character.
links.list_adds: It assigns three ornaments to three wearers, the eye, a woman and the next life, and says all three gather in one kind of person.

links.note: Kural 1014 calls modesty the ornament of the worthy; Thirikadugam calls it the ornament of a woman in love.
links.teaches: The Kural gives naanam to the saandror without regard to sex; the verse gives it to the woman, so the same virtue is, in the two books, a mark of nobility and a gendered duty.
links.list_adds: It sets the woman's modesty between the eye's kindness and learning for the next life, giving each ornament its own wearer.

links.note: Kural 402 likens the unlearned man's wish to speak to a breastless woman's desire; Thirikadugam sets the unlearned man's eager talk beside a blind man's wife's beauty and lute-music heard by one who cannot tell its modes.
links.teaches: The couplet's image locates the lack in the speaker; the verse's neighbours locate it in a missing receiver, so the pair shows unlearned speech failing both for want of substance and for want of anyone able to take it.
links.list_adds: It groups unlearned speech with beauty unseen and music unheard, making it one kind of waste with them rather than a lone figure of incapacity.

links.note: Kural 584 says a spy examines everyone, the king's servants and kin first; Thirikadugam names a secret-leaking friend, a woman without regard for honour and a rancorous servant as those called spies.
links.teaches: The couplet turns the king's surveillance inward on his own circle; the verse shows why from the other side, since those closest, friend, woman and servant, are the ones who leak.
links.list_adds: It names the household's own informers by kind, giving concrete cases of the inward danger the couplet only implies.

links.note: Kural 131 says conduct gives excellence and must be guarded above life; Thirikadugam makes joining the road of inherited conduct the third of three things that keep the path of excellence open, after letters and the service of parents.
links.teaches: Both books tie ஒழுக்கம் to விழுப்பம், but the Kural makes conduct its single source, while the verse makes it the last step of a sequence that begins with learning letters and serving parents.
links.list_adds: It orders conduct in time, after literacy and filial service, so excellence is reached by a sequence rather than by one virtue.

links.note: Kural 392 calls numbers and letters the two eyes of living beings; Thirikadugam makes learning the letters first the opening step on the path of excellence.
links.teaches: The couplet values letters as sight; the verse gives them a place in time, first, before the parents and inherited conduct, so literacy becomes the start of a moral sequence.
links.list_adds: It makes letters the first of three ordered steps (முந்தை ... பிற்பாடு), a sequence the couplet does not have.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 31 says singing to an untuned lute is very painful; Thirikadugam says song not measured to the beat is painful to hear.
links.teaches: One verse faults the pitch and the other the beat, so together they show the period held music to two measures, tuning and time, either of which failing makes song painful.

links.note: Kural 525 says one who gives and speaks sweetly is surrounded by kin layer on layer; Thirikadugam makes giving by old ties, embracing kin and gathering one's people with close words the work of the king's younger.
links.teaches: The couplet gives anyone the means to gather kin; the verse assigns that work in a royal house to the junior prince, so kin-keeping becomes a delegated office of state.
links.list_adds: It moves the kin-gathering acts into the royal household and gives them to one office, the king's younger.

links.note: Kural 523 likens the life of one who does not mingle with kin to a tank filling with water but with no bank; Thirikadugam says the wealth of one who does not help his kin perishes while seeming to exist.
links.teaches: The Kural's tank shows the water running off; the verse adds that the loss is hidden, the wealth still seems to be there, so the tank looks full while it drains.
links.list_adds: It groups kinless wealth with untended farming and a drinker's family name as three goods lost while still in sight.

links.note: Kural 1039 says land the owner does not visit sulks like a wife; Thirikadugam says the farming of one who does not tend the green crop at ripening perishes.
links.teaches: The couplet asks for the owner's steady presence; the verse names the moment when absence is fatal, the time of ripening, so neglect is located in time.
links.list_adds: It sets the untended harvest beside kinless wealth and a drinker's lineage, making all three cases of loss that looks like having.

links.note: Kural 1041 says nothing is more painful than poverty except poverty; Thirikadugam names want as the sorrow proper to human birth, beside the ghost's hunger and the beast's fear.
links.teaches: The Kural makes poverty incomparable among human pains; the verse explains its place: each kind of birth has its own sorrow and want is the human one.
links.list_adds: It sets human want beside the hunger of ghosts and the fear of beasts, so poverty becomes the human share of a sorrow common to all births.

links.note: Naladiyar 174 grants that birth is bitter but says no one would resent it given lasting friendship with the good; Thirikadugam lists the sorrow of each kind of birth with no remedy.
links.teaches: The verse itemises the bitterness of birth by kind of being; the quatrain names the one thing that makes it bearable, so the pair holds the diagnosis and the consolation apart.
links.list_adds: It divides the bitterness of birth into hunger, fear and want, by kind of birth, where the quatrain speaks of birth whole.

source_issues: 41 lines 2-3: அன்போடி stands before the dash and seems to run into line 3; it is taken as அன்போடு, 'with affection'.
45 line 3: the count word is fused with the verb (தானுமிம் மூவர்), so count_word records மூவர் and the third item stops at சிந்தியா.
46: printed without a number and numbered 46 by its place after 45; line 4 repeats the closing line of verse 14.
